title: Rome vs Florence: Which Should You Visit?
verdict: Rome for epic scale and ancient history. Florence for Renaissance art and Tuscan charm. Do both if you have 7+ days.

categories.name: Food & Dining
categories.summary: Rome has iconic street food (supplì, cacio e pepe, gelato). Florence has superior trattorias, bistecca Fiorentina, and Tuscany's wine country right outside.

categories.name: Ancient History & Art
categories.summary: Rome wins on ancient ruins (Colosseum, Forum, Pantheon). Florence wins on Renaissance art (Uffizi, David, Duomo).

categories.name: Cost
categories.summary: Florence is marginally cheaper, though both cities are mid-range for Western Europe.

categories.name: Getting Around
categories.summary: Florence is walkable in a way Rome simply isn't. Everything is within 30 minutes on foot.

categories.name: Day Trips
categories.summary: Florence wins on day trips — Siena, Cinque Terre, Pisa, Lucca, Tuscan wine country all within 1-2 hours.

categories.name: Atmosphere
categories.summary: Florence feels like an open-air Renaissance museum. Rome is a living, chaotic megacity.

categories.name: Nightlife
categories.summary: Rome has more diverse nightlife. Florence is quieter and more restaurant-focused.

faq.question: Is Rome or Florence better for a first trip to Italy?
faq.answer: Rome is the classic first-timer choice — the Colosseum, Vatican, and Trevi Fountain are bucket-list icons. But many travelers say Florence is their favorite and wish they'd spent more time there. If it's your only Italy trip, do both.

faq.question: How far apart are Rome and Florence?
faq.answer: About 280 km. The high-speed Frecciarossa train takes 1h30m–1h45m and costs €20–80 depending on when you book. Regular regional trains take 3+ hours but cost as little as €12.

faq.question: How many days do you need in each city?
faq.answer: Most travelers recommend 3–4 days in Rome and 2–3 in Florence. Rome is larger with more to see. Florence can be 'done' in 2 focused days but rewards a slower pace.

faq.question: Which city is cheaper — Rome or Florence?
faq.answer: They're comparable. Florence accommodation is slightly cheaper; Rome has more budget food options (pizza al taglio, supplì). Expect €80–150/day mid-range in both cities.

faq.question: Is Florence or Rome better for food?
faq.answer: Different strengths. Rome wins on street food (pizza al taglio, cacio e pepe, gelato). Florence wins for sit-down dining — trattorias are world-class, and Tuscany's wines and bistecca Fiorentina are legendary.

faq.question: Can you visit both Rome and Florence in one trip?
faq.answer: Absolutely — and most travelers do. The Frecciarossa connects them in 1.5 hours. A 7-day Italy trip commonly splits 3–4 days in Rome and 3 days in Florence. Fly into Rome, out of Florence (or vice versa) to avoid backtracking.

faq.question: Which city is easier to navigate?
faq.answer: Florence wins by a landslide. The historic center is compact and walkable — you can see Uffizi, Ponte Vecchio, the Duomo, and Piazza della Signoria all on foot in a morning. Rome is sprawling, has fewer metro lines, and requires more transit planning.

faq.question: Which has better day trips?
faq.answer: Florence, easily. Siena (1.5h), Cinque Terre (2h), Pisa (1h), Lucca (1.5h), Chianti wine region (45min), and Montepulciano are all doable. Rome's day trips (Pompeii, Ostia Antica, Orvieto) are also good but less varied.
